name: A money type that splits exactly
brief:
A settlement system holds money as whole pence in a `long long`, never as a `double`. Write `class Cash` with `static Cash from_pence(long long p)`, `long long pence() const`, `Cash operator+(Cash other) const`, and two harder members. `static Cash from_pounds(double pounds)` takes the nearest whole penny, half a penny going away from zero. `std::vector<Cash> split(int n) const` cuts the amount into `n` parts that add up to it exactly, each within a penny of the others. The parts a penny larger in size come first, and every part has the sign of the whole.

`from_pounds(0.29)` must give 29 pence, although `0.29 * 100` is just below 29 as a `double`. Splitting 100p three ways gives 34, 33 and 33, and -100p gives -34, -33 and -33.
constraints: $|$pounds$| \le 10^{9}$ and $1 \le n \le 1000$. Amounts in pence fit in a `long long`.
hint: `std::llround` rounds half-way away from zero. In C++ `p % n` has the sign of `p`, so for a negative amount the extra pennies are negative.

examples.note: The extra penny goes first, with the sign of the whole.

how: Submit runs 15 hidden tests. Each answer must equal the expected value. Hidden helpers convert pounds, add two amounts, and split an amount into a list of pence.
notes: A cast to `long long` truncates, so 28.999999999999996 becomes 28; rounding to the nearest penny is the fix.
`p_ / n` and `p_ % n` both round towards zero in C++, so for a negative amount the remainder is negative too.
Handing out the remainder one penny at a time keeps every part within a penny and the total exact.

planted.slip: The cast truncates, so 0.29 pounds becomes 28 pence.
Gives the whole remainder to the first part, so parts can differ by more than a penny.
Hands out the remainder only when it is positive, so a negative amount loses pennies.
